were about four percent slower than those from the
first quarter, which may point to the yeast tin having
been opened many times by then.

4   Discussion

For a baker the main result is that the time printed
in a recipe is right at one temperature only. A recipe
that says one and a half hours was probably written
in a kitchen at about 27 degrees. In a room at 20
degrees the same dough needs nearly twice as long,
and at 16 degrees close to three times as long. The
sign of doubling is the better guide, and a straight-
sided container makes it easy to judge.
   The rule of a third per four degrees is rough, and
it has limits. It was measured between 16 and 28 de-
grees. Above that the gain shrinks, and other work
with yeast suggests that somewhere beyond 35 de-
grees the rise slows down again. Below 16 degrees
we have no measurements at all. A refrigerator, at
about 4 degrees, is far outside the range, and the rule
should not be stretched to it.
   The experiment has other limits too. One flour,
one yeast and one amount of water were used. A wet-
ter dough or a wholemeal flour may respond differ-
ently. The kneading was done by one person, which
keeps the batches alike but means that we cannot
say how much kneading matters. Finally, height in
a container measures the volume of the dough and
not the amount of gas made, since some gas escapes
through the surface.

5   Conclusion

A plain wheat dough doubled in about four hours at
16 degrees Celsius and in about one hour at 32 de-
grees. Between 16 and 28 degrees every extra four de-
grees shortened the wait by roughly a third. Batches
differed from one another by about a tenth of the
waiting time, whatever the temperature. Recipes
would serve bakers in cool and warm kitchens bet-
ter if they gave the temperature at which their times
were measured, or a small table like ours.
